Best NAS for Immich and Photo Backup, Lab-Timed | ComputingForGeeks 
 Skip to content 
 ⓘ This post contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 Immich works a NAS hardest on the first day, when it runs face detection, smart search and text recognition across every photo you own. After that, a phone backing up a few dozen shots a night barely registers. So we sized this list of the best NAS for Immich by that first import, not by the daily sync. We tested Immich v3.3.3 on October 20, 2026 on a 4-core, 8 GB Proxmox VM, timed every machine learning job on a 497-photo library and logged the memory each container used.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 175925 
 We didn’t have any of these NAS boxes on the bench, so the hardware notes come from maker spec sheets and the Immich issue tracker, and we name each source where we use it. Prices are from Amazon US on the same day. The measured part is Immich itself: what it needs, where it spends its time, and why more cores matter more than any setting you can change.
 NAS Best for CPU RAM, stock / max Price, Oct 20 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Most households Pentium Gold 8505, 5 cores 8 GB / 64 GB $656.99 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Pro Big libraries on CPU Core i3-N305, 8 cores 8 GB / 32 GB $594.99 
 UGREEN DXP2800 Best value N100, 4 cores 8 GB / 16 GB $389.99 
 Synology DS425+ Staying on DSM Celeron J4125, 4 cores 2 GB / 6 GB $579.99 
 QNAP TS-264-8G Two bays with a PCIe slot Celeron N5095, 4 cores 8 GB / 16 GB $469.00 
 Beelink ME mini DIY all-flash N150, 4 cores 12 GB, soldered $359.00 
 Check the NAS against the Immich floor
 Immich’s requirements page sets a minimum of 6 GB of RAM and 2 cores, and recommends 8 GB and 4 cores. Since v3 the machine learning container on x86 also needs an x86-64-v2 CPU, which every pick here meets. The rule that catches NAS owners is storage: the Postgres database should sit on local SSD and “never a network share of any kind”, so a box with an M.2 slot has a real advantage.
 Our VM showed why the RAM floor is set where it is. With an empty library, all four containers used about 1,350 MiB at idle, and about 2,430 MiB at idle once the photos were in. At default settings the highest peak was 2,547 MiB during OCR, and running face detection at concurrency 4 pushed it to 2,620 MiB. On 8 GB that leaves room for a NAS OS beside it, but it is already past a stock 2 GB Synology. It doesn’t leave much either on a 4 GB QNAP once the vendor OS takes its share.
 Time the first import, not the daily sync
 We imported 497 public-domain NASA photos, 300 of them astronaut portraits, so face detection had real work to do. Machine learning ran CPU-only on 4 vCPUs of an Intel Core i7-6700, a 2015 desktop chip that is still faster than most of the NAS CPUs below. Expect the J4125 and N5095 boxes in particular to take longer than these figures. We re-ran the two biggest jobs once the models were cached, which removes the one-time download from the timing:
 Job, 497 photos First run, with model download Re-run, default concurrency Re-run, concurrency 4 
 Upload, metadata, thumbnails 73 s n/a n/a 
 Smart Search (CLIP) 82 s 39.1 s, 12.7 photos/s 38.9 s 
 Face detection 131 s 125.8 s, 3.95 photos/s 136.7 s 
 Face recognition (clustering) 11 s, 84 people n/a n/a 
 OCR (on by default in v3) 162 s, 3.1 photos/s n/a n/a 
 Face detection and OCR are where the time goes. Face detection kept all four cores busy, and raising it from 2 to 4 parallel jobs made it 9% slower. The peak load average rose by about half, from 4.9 to 7.6, and the ML container grew from about 800 MiB to 1.1 GiB. Smart Search didn’t speed up either. OCR ran at its default of one job and used about half the CPU, and we didn’t test it at higher settings. So don’t turn the face detection or Smart Search concurrency up on a 4-core NAS. More cores, or a working accelerator, is the lever that moves the number.
 Scaled linearly from those figures, a first import on this class of CPU takes roughly 2.2 hours for 10,000 photos, 11 hours for 50,000 and about 45 hours for 200,000. Treat that as an order of magnitude, because phone photos are bigger than our test files and every NAS CPU differs from the one we used. It fits a maintainer’s warning that a 750,000-asset library can take weeks on minimal hardware .
 Choose the NAS by library size
 Library size decides how much the CPU matters, because the first import scales with it and everything after that is light. Here is how we would split the picks, using the lab timings above:
 Library Estimated first import on 4 cores What to buy 
 About 10,000 photos An evening, about 2 h UGREEN DXP2800, or a DS425+ with the RAM upgrade if a slower import is fine 
 About 50,000 photos Overnight, about 11 h UGREEN DXP4800 Plus or TerraMaster F4-425 Pro 
 200,000 photos or more About 2 days F4-425 Pro with 16 to 32 GB, or remote ML on a desktop GPU 
 The last row has a way out that most buyers miss. Immich can send its machine learning jobs to a remote ML container on another machine, so a desktop with a GPU can do the first pass and the NAS takes over afterwards. That’s worth doing once for a big library, rather than paying for a faster NAS you’ll only need for two days.
 Buy a NAS that runs Immich well
 Every box below meets the RAM floor as shipped or with one cheap stick and has Intel graphics for Quick Sync video transcoding. The NAS units run Docker from the vendor OS, and the Beelink runs whatever OS you install. Each comes with the one trade-off we’d want to know before buying it.
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus: best overall
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus (image: UGREEN), sold by UGREEN GROUP LIMITED 
 The DXP4800 Plus is $656.99 without drives. It has four bays, a five-core Pentium Gold 8505, 8 GB of DDR5 that goes to 64 GB, two M.2 slots for the database and thumbnails, and a 10GbE port beside a 2.5GbE one. It is the only pick with 10GbE and a 64 GB memory ceiling, and it still puts the database on NVMe.
 Its Intel graphics can run Immich’s OpenVINO backend, but the hardware acceleration page still calls that feature experimental, and we could not test it on this box. Plan the first import as CPU-only and treat any speedup as a bonus. Our 4-bay NAS guide covers its drive bays, UGOS and the warranty terms in more depth.
 Check price on Amazon 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Pro: best for big libraries
 TerraMaster F4-425 Pro (image: TerraMaster), sold by TERRAMASTER 
 The F4-425 Pro with the Core i3-N305 is $594.99, and its eight cores go straight at the jobs our lab showed were slow. It ships with 8 GB, takes up to 32 GB in one SO-DIMM slot, and has three M.2 slots and two 5GbE ports. If you’re bringing 50,000 or more photos across from Google Photos or iCloud, this is the box that shortens that first import the most on CPU alone.
 Software is the catch. A TerraMaster FAQ says that installing another operating system voids the warranty , so the safe plan is to stay on TOS and run Immich in its Docker app. That is fine for Immich, which only needs Docker Compose. Reports differ on Unraid: a January 2025 NASCompares report said TerraMaster had changed its policy so that Unraid no longer voids the warranty, so ask TerraMaster before you switch the OS.
 Check price on Amazon 
 UGREEN DXP2800: best value
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800 (image: UGREEN), sold by UGREEN GROUP LIMITED 
 The DXP2800 is $389.99 for two bays, a four-core N100, 8 GB of DDR5, two M.2 slots and a 2.5GbE port. For one household backing up phones, that covers Immich’s recommended spec with the database on NVMe and two drives in a mirror for the photos. Memory tops out at 16 GB, so it is not the box for a library that keeps growing for years.
 Expect the first import to load it fully. An owner of an N100 DXP4800 with 8 GB reported that a bulk import pushed the load past 16 and made the box unresponsive until he pinned CPUs and capped the ML container. We saw the same pattern on our VM, where the ML container used every core it had. Let it finish overnight and it settles down.
 Check price on Amazon 
 Synology DS425+: for people staying on DSM
 Synology DiskStation DS425+ (image: Synology), sold by Amazon.com 
 The DS425+ is $579.99, but it ships with 2 GB of RAM, a third of Immich’s minimum, and Synology’s datasheet caps it at 6 GB with one extra 4 GB module. The OWC 4 GB module at $34.99 gets it to exactly that floor, but the same datasheet warns that Synology “will not provide complete product warranty or technical support” with non-Synology memory. Synology’s own 4 GB module was only on offer from a third-party seller at $229.99 when we checked.
 Its Celeron J4125 is the slowest CPU on this list. A regression in earlier releases broke OpenVINO on a DS423+ with the same chip, among other Intel GPUs, until it was closed as fixed in late September 2026. M.2 storage pools also need Synology-verified SSDs, which matters if you want the database on NVMe. Run Immich CPU-only and it works, but buy it for DSM, not for Immich; if DSM isn’t the draw, our Synology alternatives guide compares the boxes that replace it. The 2-bay DS225+ at $364.99 has the same CPU and memory limits and no M.2 slots.
 Check price on Amazon 
 QNAP TS-264-8G: two bays with an upgrade path
 QNAP TS-264 (image: QNAP), sold by Amazon.com 
 The TS-264-8G is $469 with 8 GB, two M.2 slots, two 2.5GbE ports and a PCIe Gen 3 x2 slot on QNAP’s spec sheet for an expansion card later. Memory goes to 16 GB, and QNAP says to use its own modules. Pick it among the 2-bay boxes if you want to add faster networking without replacing the box.
 Its Celeron N5095 is one of the two slowest chips here, ahead of only the J4125, and Jasper Lake has had OpenVINO trouble. One owner hit “out of GPU resources” in face detection until he switched to a smaller face model , and the same regression that hit the J4125 also broke OpenVINO on Jasper Lake before the fix. Plan for CPU-only and a slower first import than the N100 or N305 boxes.
 Check price on Amazon 
 Beelink ME mini: the DIY all-flash route
 Beelink ME mini (image: Beelink); the linked listing is sold by THYPC-Beelink 
 The ME mini with an N150 and 12 GB of soldered LPDDR5 is $359, and it suits a reader who wants to run TrueNAS or Unraid instead of a vendor OS. It has six M.2 slots, with Beelink recommending slot 4 for the system drive and listing up to 24 TB in total, plus two 2.5GbE ports. It ships with Windows 11 Home, so you replace the OS before anything else. The TrueNAS Immich app sits in the Community catalog, and our DIY NAS guide covers the build, with TrueNAS versus Unraid for the OS choice.
 Cost per terabyte is the trade-off. With no hard drive bays, a 200,000-photo library on SSDs gets expensive fast, and the 12 GB can’t be upgraded. The Amazon listing in stock when we checked was sold by THYPC-Beelink, while a Beelink-sold listing for the 2 TB model showed a later availability date, so check the seller before you order.
 Check price on Amazon 
 Avoid these three for Immich
 These boxes look like obvious picks, and each has a reason we left it out:
 NAS Price, Oct 20 Why we skipped it 
 UGREEN DXP4800 GT $659.99 AMD Ryzen R2514: no OpenVINO, and the ROCm path is unverified on this chip 
 QNAP TS-462A-4G $529.00 Ships with 4 GB, below Immich’s 6 GB minimum 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus $649.99 to $699.99 Costs more than the F4-425 Pro with half the cores 
 As a dual-10GbE NAS the DXP4800 GT is good, but for Immich it runs machine learning on four CPU cores at a higher price than the DXP4800 Plus. If faster networking matters more than ML, our all-flash NVMe NAS guide is the better starting point.
 Put the database on local NVMe
 Immich’s release ships an example .env file that sets two paths: one for your photos and one for the Postgres database. On a NAS, those two belong on different storage, and this is the one setting worth changing before the first container starts. Check both lines in the file you downloaded:
 grep -n LOCATION .env 
 In the stock file from the release we tested, they read:
 4:UPLOAD_LOCATION=./library
7:DB_DATA_LOCATION=./postgres 
 On a Synology, the NVMe pool needs Synology-verified SSDs. Change the two paths in this order before you start Immich:
 Create a folder on the NVMe pool for the database
 Point DB_DATA_LOCATION at that NVMe folder
 Point UPLOAD_LOCATION at a share on the hard drive pool
 Start the stack with docker compose up -d
 Moving the database after a big import is a much bigger job than setting the path first. If you add an external library on a network share, leave library watching off. One owner found that watching about 90,000 files over SMB caused a storm of filesystem metadata calls that stalled every Immich queue. Our Immich install guide walks through the full compose setup on a plain Linux host.
 Check where the models run
 A NAS that claims OpenVINO support only speeds up Immich if the machine learning container actually uses the iGPU, and it falls back to the CPU quietly when it can’t. The container log shows which backends the image offers each time it loads a model. On our CPU-only VM, this was the check:
 docker logs immich_machine_learning 2>&1 | grep -A1 " Setting execution providers " | head -5 
 With the stock image, only the CPU backend was available. The container logs in UTC, which is why the timestamps read October 19:
 [10/19/26 22:59:34] INFO Setting execution providers to
 ['CPUExecutionProvider'], in descending order of
--
[10/19/26 23:00:42] INFO Setting execution providers to
 ['CPUExecutionProvider'], in descending order of 
 To try the iGPU on an Intel box, the Immich docs switch the container to the OpenVINO build in four steps:
 Download hwaccel.ml.yml next to docker-compose.yml
 Add -openvino to the machine learning image tag
 Uncomment extends and set service to openvino
 Recreate the container with docker compose up -d
 Don’t trust that same log line afterwards. The OpenVINO image always lists OpenVINOExecutionProvider first, and the Immich source quietly sets the OpenVINO device to the CPU when it finds no GPU. The reliable test is the one the docs give: watch the iGPU with intel_gpu_top while a Smart Search job runs. It needs a Linux shell on the host, or a container with /dev/dri, and on Debian and Ubuntu it comes in the intel-gpu-tools package:
 sudo intel_gpu_top 
 The Render/3D engine should climb while the job runs and drop back when it ends. On DSM, QTS or TOS, where that tool isn’t available, read the log instead. Set IMMICH_LOG_LEVEL=debug in .env, run docker compose up -d to recreate the containers, and look for ‘device_type’: ‘GPU.0’ in the execution provider options instead of ‘CPU’. If the GPU stays idle, one owner found that the plain ML container was still running , so check the image tag with docker ps before you blame the hardware.

 Quick Summary (TL;DR): 
For Immich, do not choose a NAS Price AliExpress price only by drive capacity. Immich currently requires at least 6GB RAM and recommends 8GB , while thumbnail generation, Smart Search, facial recognition, video transcoding and PostgreSQL create a much more application-heavy workload than simple photo file storage. Our strongest all-round choice is the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Price : Intel 8505, 8GB DDR5 expandable to 64GB, Intel Quick Sync, two M.2 slots, four HDD bays and built-in 10GbE. The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus Price is an excellent value alternative because it starts with 16GB DDR5, uses the newer Intel N150 , has three M.2 slots and dual 5GbE. The QNAP TS-464 is attractive if you prefer the mature QTS/Container Station ecosystem and Intel Quick Sync, although its 16GB official RAM ceiling limits very large application stacks. The Synology DS925+ is our backup-first choice because DSM, Btrfs, ECC RAM, Hyper Backup, Snapshot Replication and DX525 expansion are excellent for protecting a family archive—but its stock 4GB RAM is below Immich’s current minimum, so upgrade it before running Immich, and its Ryzen V1500B lacks Intel Quick Sync. For irreplaceable family photos, the NAS AliExpress price itself is not the backup: Immich explicitly recommends a 3-2-1 strategy and requires both the database and original photo/video files for a complete restore.
 Best NAS for Immich and Family Photo Backups: Shortlist
 NAS AliExpress price Why it fits Immich Main limitation Best for 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Intel 8505, 8GB→64GB, Quick Sync, 2 M.2, 10GbE Younger NAS software ecosystem Best all-round Immich + Docker server 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus Intel N150 , 16GB→32GB, 3 M.2, dual 5GbE Less CPU headroom than 8505 Best value / strong out-of-box RAM 
 QNAP TS-464 N5095, 8GB→16GB, Quick Sync, Container Station, 2 M.2 16GB official RAM ceiling Mature Docker/ NAS platform 
 Synology DS925+ ECC RAM, Btrfs, snapshots, Hyper Backup, 4→9 bays 4GB stock RAM is below Immich minimum; no Intel iGPU Backup-first family archive 
 Immich Is Not Just a Folder of JPEGs
 A traditional photo NAS can be extremely light on CPU. You copy files to a shared folder, browse them occasionally and back them up.
 Immich does much more:
 PostgreSQL database operations.
 Thumbnail generation.
 Video transcoding.
 Smart Search.
 Facial recognition.
 Metadata extraction.
 Mobile uploads.
 Background jobs after large imports.
 That means the best Immich NAS is partly a storage appliance and partly a small application server.
 Current Immich Hardware Requirements
 Immich currently lists:
 Minimum RAM: 6GB.
 Recommended RAM: 8GB.
 Minimum CPU: 2 cores.
 Recommended CPU: 4 cores.
 Architecture: amd64 or arm64.
 Recommended production deployment: Docker Compose on a Linux/*nix-style system.
 Those are minimum/recommended requirements for running Immich—not a promise that 8GB is ideal for a huge library while the same NAS runs ten other containers.
 How Much RAM Should an Immich NAS Have?
 For a dedicated or lightly shared Immich NAS , 8GB is the sensible floor because it matches Immich’s current recommendation.
 We would size more generously when the NAS also runs:
 Nextcloud.
 Plex or Jellyfin.
 Home Assistant services.
 Several PostgreSQL databases.
 Virtual machines.
 Large Docker stacks.
 Other machine-learning applications.
 For that type of combined server, 16GB is much more comfortable and 32GB+ can be useful. Immich’s machine-learning service can also consume additional memory as models are loaded; Immich specifically cautions that increasing machine-learning workers duplicates models in memory.
 Photo Library Size: Start with Your Originals
 Do not start by asking “How many terabytes does Immich need?” Start with your existing photo/video archive.
 required capacity
≈ current originals
+ future annual growth
+ generated Immich data
+ free-space headroom
+ RAID overhead 
 A simple example:
 80,000 photos × average 7MB
≈ 560GB
2,000 videos × average 300MB
≈ 600GB
Current originals
≈ 1.16TB 
 Those file sizes are only an illustration. Your phone’s HEIC photos, DSLR RAW files and 4K/8K videos can make the real number much smaller or dramatically larger.
 Video Usually Drives Photo-Library Growth
 Modern smartphone video grows much faster than still-photo storage.
 A household that takes a lot of 4K video can add more storage in one year than many years of JPEG/HEIC photos.
 When forecasting five-year capacity, separate:
 Phone photos.
 RAW camera files.
 Phone videos.
 Action-camera/drone video.
 Scanned family archives.
 Then add realistic free-space headroom rather than buying a NAS that starts at 90% full.
 Immich Originals and Generated Data Are Different
 Immich stores the uploaded originals plus generated content such as thumbnails and encoded videos.
 The original photos and videos are irreplaceable. Generated thumbnails and encoded videos can be regenerated if necessary, although doing so may take substantial time on a large library.
 This distinction matters for backup design: originals and database metadata deserve the highest protection, while generated content can be treated differently if storage budget is tight.
 The Database Is Critical
 Immich stores file paths and user metadata in PostgreSQL. The project explicitly warns that it does not simply rescan the main library folder to reconstruct all application state.
 A proper backup therefore needs:
 The original assets.
 The Immich database backup.
 Configuration required to recreate the deployment.
 Immich’s built-in database backups do not contain the photos and videos themselves.
 Immich Explicitly Recommends 3-2-1 Backup
 For family photos, this should be treated as a requirement rather than an optional optimisation.
 3 copies of important data
2 different storage media / systems
1 copy off-site 
 A four-drive RAID 5 or RAID 6 array is still only one copy.
 RAID protects availability after a drive failure. It does not protect you from accidental deletion, filesystem corruption, ransomware, theft, fire or a catastrophic NAS failure.
 Best Overall: UGREEN DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus is our strongest all-round Immich NAS because it combines a modern Intel application platform with conventional four-bay bulk storage.
 Intel Pentium Gold 8505.
 5 cores / 6 threads.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 8GB DDR5 included.
 Up to 64GB RAM.
 4 SATA bays.
 2 M.2 NVMe slots.
 1 × 10GbE.
 1 × 2.5GbE.
 Docker support in UGOS Pro.
 The 8GB factory configuration already meets Immich’s current recommended RAM level.
 The main benefit is headroom: if the photo server later becomes an Immich + Nextcloud + Plex + Home Assistant + database machine, 32GB or 64GB memory remains possible.
 Why Intel Quick Sync Helps Immich
 Immich supports Intel Quick Sync Video for hardware-accelerated video transcoding.
 This can reduce CPU load when Immich creates compatible versions of uploaded videos.
 Immich currently describes hardware transcoding as experimental and notes that hardware-encoded output may be larger and lower quality than software encoding at similar settings. Treat acceleration as a useful performance feature, not a requirement for every library.
 Machine Learning Acceleration Is Separate from Video Acceleration
 Smart Search and facial recognition use Immich’s machine-learning service.
 Immich currently supports several experimental hardware-acceleration backends including CUDA, ROCm and OpenVINO for supported Intel GPUs.
 Do not assume that every NAS Intel iGPU will automatically accelerate every Immich machine-learning model. Verify the exact GPU, container access and current Immich backend support.
 If local ML is too slow, Immich also supports running the machine-learning service on a separate remote machine . This can be a better architecture than replacing a perfectly good storage NAS.
 Best Value: TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 The F4-425 Plus is unusually well configured for Immich out of the box:
 Intel N150 .
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 16GB DDR5 included.
 Up to 32GB RAM.
 4 SATA bays.
 3 M.2 PCIe 3.0 x1 slots.
 2 × 5GbE.
 Btrfs / EXT4.
 Docker-based Container Manager in TOS 7.
 Sixteen gigabytes of factory RAM means there is no immediate memory upgrade for a normal Immich deployment, and the three M.2 slots give you useful flexibility for application/database storage.
 The N150 is not as powerful as UGREEN’s 8505 for heavy mixed workloads, but it is a very sensible low-power photo-server platform.
 Best Mature Intel/Docker Platform: QNAP TS-464
 The TS-464 remains attractive because QNAP combines Intel graphics with an established container/storage platform.
 Intel N5095.
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 Intel UHD Graphics / Quick Sync.
 8GB DDR4 on current 8G model.
 Up to 16GB officially supported.
 4 SATA bays.
 2 M.2 PCIe Gen3 x1.
 2 × 2.5GbE.
 PCIe expansion slot.
 Container Station.
 The current 8GB version matches Immich’s recommended memory level.
 The 16GB official ceiling is enough for Immich plus a moderate set of containers, but it is the main reason we prefer UGREEN for a NAS expected to become a much larger home-lab server.
 Best Backup-First Platform: Synology DS925+
 The DS925+ is not our fastest Immich application server, but it may be the most attractive storage platform for a family archive.
 AMD Ryzen V1500B, 4 cores / 8 threads.
 4GB ECC DDR4 included.
 Up to 32GB ECC RAM.
 4 SATA bays.
 2 M.2 slots.
 2 × 2.5GbE.
 Btrfs.
 Hyper Backup.
 Snapshot Replication.
 Expansion to 9 total bays with DX525.
 There is one immediate Immich problem: the stock 4GB RAM is below Immich’s current 6GB minimum . Upgrade the DS925+ to at least 8GB before considering an Immich Docker deployment.
 The Ryzen V1500B also lacks Intel Quick Sync, so video transcoding will not have the same Intel hardware path as UGREEN, TerraMaster or QNAP.
 Why Synology Can Still Be the Best Family-Photo Choice
 If protecting the family archive matters more than maximising Immich indexing speed, DSM provides an excellent surrounding storage ecosystem.
 Btrfs snapshots.
 Snapshot Replication.
 Hyper Backup to local, remote and cloud destinations.
 ECC memory.
 Storage expansion.
 Synology Drive/Photos as separate first-party tools.
 You can also separate the roles: use the Synology as the protected photo repository and run Immich’s application or machine-learning compute elsewhere.
 The Best Architecture May Be Mini PC + NAS
 Immich supports remote machine learning, which makes split compute/storage particularly attractive.
 NAS
├── originals
├── database storage / backups
└── snapshots
 Mini PC / server
├── Immich application
├── Quick Sync video
└── machine learning 
 This architecture lets the storage array remain stable for many years while compute hardware is upgraded independently.
 It is especially sensible when you want NVIDIA CUDA or a faster Intel GPU for machine learning without buying a completely new NAS.
 Put PostgreSQL and Immich Application Data on SSD Where Practical
 The original photo files are mostly large sequential data. PostgreSQL, thumbnails and application metadata are much more random-I/O heavy.
 A useful hybrid layout is:
 HDD RAID pool
├── Immich originals
├── family archive
└── backups
NVMe / SSD pool
├── PostgreSQL
├── Docker data
├── thumbnails
└── application data 
 This can make Immich feel much more responsive without paying to store every original photo and video on flash.
 Do You Need 10GbE for Immich?
 Usually not for day-to-day family use.
 Photo browsing and mobile uploads do not need 10GbE.
 Faster networking becomes useful when:
 Importing a multi-terabyte existing library.
 Backing up large RAW/video collections.
 Several users upload large video files simultaneously.
 The NAS also serves workstation storage.
 You restore the entire library after a failure.
 For most homes, 2.5GbE is already comfortable. Do not choose a NAS purely because its Ethernet number is larger.
 Four Bays Are Usually Better Than Two for a Growing Photo Archive
 A two-bay RAID 1 system is simple and perfectly valid for a smaller family library.
 Four bays provide more options:
 RAID 5 for more capacity efficiency.
 RAID 6 for dual-drive tolerance.
 More incremental growth.
 Larger usable capacity without buying the biggest available HDDs.
 If you expect a large photo/video archive to grow for five or more years, four bays are usually the more comfortable starting point.
 RAID Is Not the Photo Backup
 This deserves repetition because family photos are irreplaceable.
 RAID protects against a failed disk. It does not protect against:
 Deleting the wrong album.
 Malware/ransomware.
 Application/database corruption.
 NAS theft.
 Fire/flood.
 Power-event damage.
 Administrator mistakes.
 The NAS needs another backup.
 A Practical Immich 3-2-1 Layout
 Copy 1
Primary NAS
Immich originals + database
Copy 2
USB HDD / second NAS
versioned local backup
Copy 3
off-site NAS / cloud / rotated external drive
irreplaceable originals + database backup 
 You do not necessarily need to back up generated thumbnails and encoded videos to every tier because Immich can regenerate them, but backing up the complete upload location makes recovery faster.
 Back Up the Database Before the Filesystem When Live
 Immich recommends stopping the server while making a consistent backup where possible.
 If the service must remain online, Immich recommends backing up the database first and filesystem second . This avoids a restored database referencing files that are missing from an older filesystem copy.
 That ordering detail is easy to miss and is exactly why a generic “copy the photo folder” backup is not enough.
 Test a Restore Before Trusting the Backup
 A backup job that reports “success” is not the same as a tested recovery.
 At least periodically verify that you can:
 Read the backup media.
 Locate a recent database dump.
 Recover original files.
 Recreate the Docker configuration.
 Restore into a test environment.
 Immich now provides database restore workflows through the web interface and onboarding process, which makes recovery easier—but the asset files still need to exist.
 External Libraries Need Their Own Backup Plan
 Immich can index external libraries stored outside its normal upload structure.
 That is useful when you already have an organised photo archive on the NAS.
 However, Immich metadata such as album membership or descriptions for external assets is still stored in the Immich database rather than written back into every source file.
 You therefore need both the external photo files and the Immich database to recover the complete application state.
 Do Not Edit Immich’s Managed Files Directly

 No. The vendor apps (Synology Photos, Qfile Pro, QuMagie) and Immich back up automatically for free if you have the matching server. PhotoSync's automatic transfers are in its Premium tier, which has a lifetime option as well as a subscription.

Mobile Backup | Immich 
 Skip to main content 
 On this page 
 Overview ​ 
 Immich supports uploading photos and videos from your mobile device to the server automatically.
 When backup is enabled, Immich will upload new photos and videos from selected albums when you open or resume the app, as well as periodically in the background.
 General Features ​ 
 Backup albums selection ​ 
 You can select which albums on your mobile device to back up to the server. You can also exclude specific albums (by double-tapping on them) from being backed up. This is useful for iOS users since assets can belong to multiple albums. For example, you may want to back up all assets except those in the "Videos" album.
 Deduplication ​ 
 When you first select albums for backup, Immich calculates a checksum for each file's content. This checksum identifies assets already on the server—whether uploaded via CLI, web interface, or another device. Files matching existing assets are skipped, preventing duplicate uploads and saving bandwidth.
 Networking requirements ​ 
 By default, Immich will only upload photos and videos when connected to Wi-Fi. You can change this behavior in the backup settings page.
 Backup album synchronization ​ 
 When enabled, Immich automatically creates albums on the server that mirror the albums on your mobile device. Photos and videos are organized into these server-side albums to match your device's album structure, making it easy to find and browse your content the same way you do on your phone.
 This is a one-way sync from your device to the server. You can enable this feature at any time and use the Reorganize into album button to backfill existing uploads into their corresponding albums.
 Platform Specific Features ​ 
 Android ​ 
 It is a well-known problem that some Android models are very strict with battery optimization settings, which can cause a problem with the background worker. Please visit Don't kill my app for a guide on disabling this setting on your phone.
 You can allow the background task to run only when the device is charging.
 You can set the minimum delay from the time a photo is taken to when the background upload task will run.
 iOS ​ 
 You must enable Background App Refresh for the app to work in the background. You can enable it in the Settings app under General > Background App Refresh.
 iOS automatically manages background tasks; the app cannot control when the background upload task will run. The more frequently you open the app, the more often background tasks will run.
 iCloud Backup ​ 
 Local albums containing assets from iCloud and marked for backup in Immich will be pulled from iCloud and temporarily stored in the app's cache folder. Once the hashing and uploading process is completed, the temporary files will be emptied.
 This process may consume additional data and storage space on your device, especially if you have a large number of iCloud photos and videos. Please ensure you have sufficient storage space and monitor your data usage if you are not connected to Wi-Fi.

 Immich is free and open source, and its feature list rivals the big cloud services: timeline, maps, face recognition, search, sharing. The iOS app backs up in the background (iOS decides when) and Immich never modifies your originals. You run the server yourself, typically in Docker on a NAS or home server, as many Unraid, TrueNAS, Synology and QNAP owners do. Photos go into Immich's own library rather than a plain SMB share you choose. There's an optional paid supporter licence, but no features are paywalled.
 9. Nextcloud: if you already run it
 Best for: households already using Nextcloud for files and calendars.
 The free Nextcloud iOS app has auto upload for photos and videos into your Nextcloud server, and uploads Live Photos as separate .heic and .mov files. Users report mixed reliability for background uploads on iOS, which has improved in recent versions. Nextcloud can store data on SMB via its External Storage feature, but the phone talks to Nextcloud, not to the share. It's a lot of infrastructure to run just for photo backup, but excellent if it's already there.
 How to choose
 I want plain originals in a folder on any NAS or PC, no account: SMBDrop, or the Files app if you're happy doing it manually.
 I want a photo library experience and I own a Synology or QNAP: Synology Photos or QuMagie/Qfile Pro.
 I want a photo platform and I'm happy self-hosting: Immich.
 I want one app for NAS, cloud and computer, with lots of triggers: PhotoSync.
 I want a general network file manager: FE File Explorer or Owlfiles.
 Whatever you choose, a NAS copy isn't a complete backup on its own. Keep a second copy somewhere else (an external drive or an offsite backup) and use snapshots if your NAS supports them. If you're moving off iCloud entirely, see how to back up an iPhone without iCloud .
 FAQ
 What is the best app to back up iPhone photos to a NAS?
 It depends on what you want. For untouched originals in a folder on any SMB share with no account, SMBDrop (which I make). For a photo library on a Synology, Synology Photos. For self-hosted photo management, Immich. For many destinations and automation, PhotoSync.
 Can I back up iPhone photos to a NAS for free?
 Yes. The built-in Files app can copy photos to any SMB share manually, and Synology Photos, QNAP's apps, Immich and Nextcloud are free if you have the matching server.
 Which apps keep Live Photos intact on a NAS?
 SMBDrop sends both halves. QNAP's apps and PhotoSync have options to include the video. Immich and Nextcloud back up Live Photos too. The Files app's Save to Files usually saves only the still.
 Do I need a subscription to back up iPhone photos to my NAS automatically?
 No. The vendor apps (Synology Photos, Qfile Pro, QuMagie) and Immich back up automatically for free if you have the matching server. PhotoSync's automatic transfers are in its Premium tier, which has a lifetime option as well as a subscription.

 How to Choose the Best NAS for Your Photo Backup Needs
 Picking the best NAS for photo backup comes down to four real decisions: how much storage you need, how fast your network is, what app experience you want, and whether you can commit to a 3-2-1 backup strategy. We tested every unit in this guide on the same criteria, and here is how to translate our findings into your own buying decision.
 Bays and RAID – How Much Storage You Actually Need
 Most families underestimate how fast photos accumulate. Our test household generated 8GB of new photos per month on average, which means a 4TB drive fills in under 4 years. We recommend a 2-bay NAS with two 8TB drives in RAID 1 as the minimum starting point, giving you 8TB of usable storage with one-drive fault tolerance.
 Photographers shooting RAW should jump straight to a 4-bay NAS like the Synology DS425+ or UGREEN DXP4800 Plus. Four 16TB drives in RAID 5 give you 48TB usable with one-drive redundancy, and you can swap in larger drives later as prices drop. Check our guide to external hard drives for backup for offsite copy recommendations.
 Processor and RAM – Speed for Photo Workflows
 The CPU matters more than most buyers realize. Intel Celeron and Pentium chips handle Plex transcoding and Synology Photos indexing without choking, while ARM-based processors in budget units can struggle once you load more than two apps. Our test showed a 4x speed difference in photo indexing between the Synology DS225+ and the DS223j.
 RAM affects how many concurrent tasks the NAS can handle. 1GB is enough for one user with light use, but households with multiple phones and laptops should aim for 2GB or more. The UGREEN DXP2800 with 8GB of DDR5 is the most future-proof option in the mid-range tier.
 Mobile App Ecosystem – Synology Photos vs UGREEN
 Synology Photos is the gold standard for NAS photo backup. It runs on all Synology units, supports automatic iPhone and Android backup, and includes face recognition, timeline view, and shared albums. The app has been refined over many years and works reliably in our long-term testing.
 UGREEN’s AI photo album is a newer but competitive alternative. Face and object tagging accuracy is nearly identical to Synology, and the app interface feels slightly more modern. The trade-off is a smaller app ecosystem, no Docker support on entry-level units, and fewer third-party integrations.
 3-2-1 Backup Strategy with NAS
 NAS alone is not a backup. RAID protects against drive failure, but not against fire, theft, or accidental deletion. The 3-2-1 rule means three copies of your data, on two different media types, with one copy offsite. Here is how a NAS fits into that strategy.
 Copy one is your primary NAS with RAID. Copy two is a USB external drive you sync weekly using Hyper Backup or UGREEN’s backup tool. Copy three is an offsite cloud backup to Backblaze B2, Wasabi, or even a friend’s house running a second NAS. The Synology DS124 makes a great offsite target.
 Drive Compatibility and Noise Considerations
 Synology dropped its first-party drive requirement in 2024, so any NAS-grade drive (Seagate Ironwolf, WD Red Plus, Toshiba N300) works in the DS225+ and DS425+. The UGREEN units accept standard NAS drives without compatibility lists.
 Noise is often overlooked. We measured all 8 NAS units at 1 meter distance and found a 10 dB spread between the quietest (Synology DS124) and loudest (UGREEN DXP4800 Plus under load). If your NAS will live in a living area, prioritize quieter units.
 Best NAS for Photo Backup FAQs
 Which NAS is best for photo backup?
 The Synology DS225+ is the best NAS for photo backup for most people. It pairs an Intel CPU with Synology Photos, delivers 282 MB/s transfer speeds, and includes a 3-year warranty. For tighter budgets, the Synology DS223j covers 90% of the same experience on gigabit networking.
 Can I use my NAS to back up photos?
 Yes. A NAS connects to your router via Ethernet and creates a shared storage location that all devices on your network can access. Install hard drives, set up the NAS operating system (DSM or UGREEN OS), and use the mobile app to automatically backup photos over Wi-Fi or cellular.
 What is the best NAS app for storing photos?
 Synology Photos is the best NAS app for storing photos. It supports automatic iPhone and Android backup, face recognition, timeline view, location clustering, and shared albums. The app runs on all current Synology DiskStation models and processes everything locally on your network.
 Which NAS is best for backing up iPhone photos?
 The Synology DS225+ is the best NAS for iPhone photo backup because Synology Photos integrates deeply with iOS permissions and supports automatic upload over Wi-Fi only. The UGREEN DH2300 is the easiest to set up if you want a beginner-friendly experience.
 What is the best backup system for photos?
 The best backup system for photos follows the 3-2-1 rule: three copies on two different media types with one copy offsite. Use a NAS as your primary copy, a USB external drive as your secondary, and either cloud storage (Backblaze B2) or a second NAS at another location as your offsite copy.
 Final Verdict – Which NAS Should You Buy for Photo Backup
 After 90 days of testing 8 NAS units with real photo libraries, our recommendations come down to who you are. If you want the best NAS for photo backup with no compromises, the Synology DS225+ is our editor’s choice and the unit we use ourselves. The Intel CPU, Synology Photos app, and 3-year warranty justify the price.
 If you are on a budget, the Synology DS223j covers most of the same photo backup experience on slower gigabit networking. For beginners who have never set up a NAS before, the UGREEN DH2300 is the easiest entry point with the best AI photo organization. Photographers managing large RAW libraries should jump straight to the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus for 10GbE speeds and 144TB capacity.
 Whichever NAS you choose in 2026, commit to the 3-2-1 backup strategy. One NAS in one location is a single point of failure, and no one wants to lose their photo library twice. Pick up a USB drive for local backup and a cheap cloud subscription for offsite, and your memories are safer than they have ever been on a phone alone.

 Synology Photos is the most polished NAS photo application available in 2026. It provides a familiar chronological timeline, automatic organization by date and location, shared family albums, and face recognition that runs entirely on your NAS hardware. It is available as a free package on any Synology NAS and works with both the Synology Photos mobile app and any web browser.

What you give up is Google's AI search quality — Google's "find photos of me at the beach in 2022" natural language search is genuinely impressive, and Synology Photos is not quite there yet, though it is improving. For families paying for multiple iCloud or Google One plans, the NAS pays for itself in two to three years of avoided subscription costs.
 Mobile backup behavior is important to understand. Synology Photos on iOS backs up photos when the app is open or in the background with background app refresh enabled. Unlike Google Photos which runs silently and aggressively in the background, you may occasionally find a week's worth of photos waiting to sync when you open the Synology Photos app. On Android, background sync is somewhat more reliable. It handles automatic backup of your camera roll, creates albums, lets you browse your entire library, and supports shared albums with family members who each have their own NAS user account. Setup takes about ten minutes: install the Synology Photos package on the NAS, create user accounts, and log in on each phone.

 Synology Photos runs face detection and recognition on the NAS itself using a neural network model included with DSM. It progressively scans your library after import, grouping detected faces into clusters that you can label with names. Once labeled, it can find photos of that person across your entire library. The process takes time for large libraries — a library of 50,000 photos can take several days to fully index on a DS224+ — but it runs in the background without interrupting normal use.

 QNAP's QuMagie uses a similar on-device AI approach with competitive face and scene recognition.  RAW Files and Video: Storage Planning for Serious Photographers
 Smartphone photos average 3–8 MB each in JPEG or HEIC format. That sounds manageable until you realize a family of four shooting 10,000 photos per year generates 30–80 GB annually in phone photos alone. Add video and you can easily hit 200–500 GB per year from smartphones.
 Serious photographers with DSLR or mirrorless cameras face a much larger storage challenge. RAW files from modern cameras range from 20 MB for entry-level APS-C cameras to 90 MB for high-megapixel full-frame sensors (Sony A7RV, Nikon Z8). A single shooting day producing 1,000 RAW files can generate 30–90 GB of data. Photographers who shoot both RAW and JPEG doubles the storage requirement.
 For photographers with large RAW libraries, 2.5G Ethernet makes a real difference during import. Copying 50 GB of RAW files over gigabit Ethernet takes around seven minutes at 100 MB/s; over 2.5G it drops to under three minutes at 250 MB/s. This is why the QNAP TS-264 with dual 2.5G ports is particularly appealing for photographers — faster imports mean less time waiting and more time editing.
 For storage sizing, a reasonable starting point is 2 TB for smartphone-only families, 4–8 TB for mixed smartphone and entry-level camera users, and 8–20+ TB for working photographers or serious amateurs with years of RAW archives. Always leave 20% headroom on your volume and plan your RAID strategy accordingly: RAID 1 (mirroring) on a 2-bay gives you one drive's worth of usable space; RAID 5 on a 4-bay gives you three drives' worth.

Each family member gets their own NAS user account with their own Personal Space (visible only to them) alongside a Shared Space that the whole family can see. Photo albums can be shared with specific users or via a public link with optional password protection.
 For remote access, Synology QuickConnect is the easiest option — it creates a relay connection through Synology's servers so you can access your NAS from anywhere without port forwarding or a static IP. Performance is adequate for browsing photos but is relay-based, meaning it is slower than a direct connection. For better remote performance, configure DDNS (dynamic DNS) with port forwarding, or use the NAS's built-in VPN server so remote devices connect directly to your home network.
 Immich handles remote sharing through a link-based approach: you can share individual photos or albums via a shareable link, with optional expiration and password. Remote access for the owner is typically done through a reverse proxy or VPN — Nginx Proxy Manager running as a Docker container on the same NAS is a popular approach.
 Frequently Asked Questions

 Yes, with Synology Photos or Immich you can replicate most of what Google Photos does — automatic mobile backup, face recognition, shared albums, and a timeline view.  Yes. Synology Photos includes face recognition that runs entirely on the NAS — your photos are never sent to the cloud for analysis. The NAS indexes faces locally and groups photos by person. Recognition accuracy improves as you confirm and label faces over time.
 How much storage do I need for a photo library?
 A library of 100,000 JPEGs from a smartphone averages 300–500 GB depending on camera quality. RAW files from DSLR or mirrorless cameras are 5–10x larger per photo — a 30-megapixel RAW file is typically 25–40 MB. Serious photographers with large RAW libraries should plan for 4–20 TB or more.

 How to Choose a NAS for Photo Backup?
 Start with bay count, because it is the decision you cannot undo cheaply. Two bays with RAID 1 mirror your library, which protects against a single drive failure, but photographers frequently outgrow a 2-bay unit within one to two years. Four bays is the sensible minimum if you shoot RAW and video, because it gives you room to expand in place rather than rebuild.
 Next, look at the drive type included. Seven of the eight units here are diskless enclosures, so you will be buying two large 3.5-inch drives yourself. Only the BUFFALO LinkStation 220 ships with drives fitted, and it also hands you 2TB usable from a 4TB label because of the mirror.
 Network speed determines how long an import feels. A 1GbE port tops out around 125MB per second, which is perfectly acceptable for phone backup over home Wi-Fi but slow for a multi-terabyte archive. The DXP2800, TS-264, DS925+ and F2-425 all carry 2.5GbE, and the TS-264 and DS925+ give you two ports for link aggregation or redundancy.
 Software is where the daily experience is won or lost. Synology’s DSM and Photos app were the most approachable in our testing, with reliable Hyper Backup scheduling. UGREEN’s apps deliver real AI tagging for faces, places, text and objects. BUFFALO offers no app ecosystem at all, which is a feature or a limitation depending on how much you want to do with the box.
 Finally, consider noise and memory. The TERRAMASTER F2-425 runs at 19dB(A), which is the quietest figure here, while some QNAP owners replace fans on the TS-264 for a desk setup. On memory, 8GB is the comfortable floor for containers and a self-hosted photo server; 2GB, as on the DS223, is enough for backup and nothing ambitious.
 One last practical note for anyone moving from a phone-based library. Our guide to selecting multiple pictures in Google Photos mobile speeds up the export, and the WhatsApp photo download guide covers the messaging archive most people forget they have.
 Building a 3-2-1 Photo Backup on a NAS
 A NAS is a backup destination, not a backup strategy on its own. The 3-2-1 rule asks for three copies of your photos, on two different media types, with one copy stored offsite. A single NAS with a RAID 1 mirror satisfies the first two parts and fails the third, because the box lives in one room on one power circuit.
 Here is how we set it up. First, the NAS itself, with drives in a mirrored RAID configuration. Second, a rotating set of external drives that you store somewhere genuinely different, refreshed monthly. Third, an offsite copy: Backblaze B2 plus a NAS is the combination most recommended in photography forums, while Synology’s own C2 Backup is used more but reported as slower for very large libraries by people managing multi-terabyte sets.
 Second step is automation. On a Synology, Hyper Backup handles scheduled copies to external drives and cloud destinations. On UGREEN units, the scheduled backup targets cover the same ground. A schedule you actually leave enabled is worth more than a perfect one you set up once and forget.
 Third, migrate out of the cloud rather than duplicating it forever. Export your library with Google Takeout or an iCloud export, then import into a structured folder layout on the NAS before you cancel the subscription. The messy part is metadata, since JSON sidecar files and album structure do not always survive the move cleanly, so verify a sample of albums with map view and date sorting before you trust the copy. We recommend doing a spot check on our how to download photos to an iPad from a digital camera workflow to confirm the originals still open correctly.
 Remote access is the last piece. A vendor relay service such as QuickConnect is the easiest and the least private, a VPN is the most private and the most work, and a mesh VPN layer such as Tailscale sits in between and avoids exposing anything to the vendor. Whichever you pick, test it from mobile data before you need it in an emergency.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Which NAS is best for photo backup?
 The UGREEN DXP2800 is the best overall NAS for photo backup in our testing, because its Intel N100 processor, 8GB of DDR5 memory, 2.5GbE networking and two NVMe slots handle phone backup, RAW libraries and self-hosted tools without strain.  How many GB do 10,000 photos need?
 It depends entirely on file type. A 12-megapixel JPEG averages roughly 4MB, so 10,000 of them need about 40GB. A 24-megapixel RAW file runs closer to 50MB, which pushes 10,000 shots past 500GB. Add video and the figure climbs fast, which is why most photographers end up filling a 2-bay mirror within a year or two.
 What is the 3-2-1 backup rule for photos?
 Keep three copies of your photos, on two different types of storage, with one copy stored away from your home. A NAS with mirrored drives gives you two copies on one type of media. Add a rotating external drive stored elsewhere plus an offsite copy such as Backblaze B2 and you satisfy all three parts of the rule.
 Can a NAS replace Google Photos?
 Yes, for storage and organisation. Every unit in this guide backs up photos automatically from phones and offers search, albums and sharing. What you lose is the enormous shared infrastructure of a cloud platform, so a common approach is to run the NAS as the primary library and keep a cloud copy as the offsite element of a 3-2-1 strategy rather than cancelling cloud storage outright.
 Do I need 2.5GbE or 10GbE for photos?
 It depends on the library. A single 1GbE port moves files at about 125MB per second, which is fine for phone backup over home Wi-Fi but slow for multi-terabyte archives. Two-bay units with 2.5GbE, such as the UGREEN DXP2800, QNAP TS-264 and TERRAMASTER F2-425, cut import times noticeably. You also need a switch and adapter that support 2.5GbE on the client side.
 What is the best self-hosted photo server for a NAS?
 Immich is the most popular option and is praised for a Google Photos-like experience, though it requires technical skill to install and maintain. PhotoPrism works well on a NAS but has a less polished interface. The UGREEN DXP2800 and QNAP TS-264 have the 8GB of memory and x86 processors we would use for either, and both support Docker.
